implementation_notes: functools.cached_property turns a method into a compute-once attribute: the getter runs on the first attribute read and the result is stored as an ordinary instance attribute, so later reads never touch the function (delete the attribute to force re-acquisition). functools.cache and lru_cache memoize at call level and are the right holder for keyed acquisition ('open this path once'), though the cache is not a lock - the documentation warns that the wrapped function can run more than once when concurrent callers arrive before the first call completes. PEP 562 module __getattr__ defers submodule import until the attribute is first touched, which is the module-level form of the pattern; the PEP's own caveat is that a plain global lookup bypasses __getattr__, so internal code must go through sys.modules[__name__] to stay lazy.
pitfalls: cached_property needs an instance __dict__: it fails on classes that define __slots__ without __dict__, and the cached value is per instance (not per class), so code that expects class-level memoization gets one acquisition per object.

A plain module global does not trigger module __getattr__ - PEP 562 states that global lookups bypass it - so a lazy attribute referenced inside its own module re-imports or fails; access it as sys.modules[__name__].name.

cache and lru_cache keep strong references to arguments and results (unbounded for @cache) and are not exactly-once: two threads can both run the function, so a costly acquisition guarded only by @cache can still happen twice unless a lock is added.
Caching is per key and never invalidated: a resource that can disappear (a rewritten file, a dropped connection) stays cached forever until cache_clear() or attribute deletion.
None is ambiguous as the not-yet marker if None is also a legitimate acquired value; use a module-level sentinel object and an explicit check.
